name: Ahaziah (son of Jehoram)
title: Judah's short-reigning king
summary: Ahaziah, son of King Joram of Judah and Athaliah from Omri's dynasty, was the sixth king of Judah after the kingdom split. He came to power as the youngest of Joram's sons after all his older brothers died during a Philistine-Arabian attack, and he reigned only one year in Jerusalem. Under strong influence from his mother and advisors linked to Ahab's house, he pursued a policy marked by idolatry and Baal worship, continuing the destructive alliance between Judah and the northern kingdom of Israel's royal line. When he visited his relative King Joram of Israel at Jezreel, he was caught up in Jehu's divinely sanctioned revolt against Ahab's dynasty and killed. His sudden death had far-reaching consequences for Judah, as it paved the way for his mother Athaliah to seize power—the only known case of a female sole ruler on David's throne—and nearly wiped out the Davidic royal line.

keyEvents.title: Brothers killed – Ahaziah becomes heir to the throne
keyEvents.description: The Philistines and Arabs attacked Judah and killed all of Jehoram's older sons. Only the youngest, Ahaziah (also called Jehoahaz), survived and became heir to the throne.

keyEvents.title: Ahaziah becomes king of Judah
keyEvents.description: Ahaziah was made king of Judah after his father Jehoram died. He was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem.

keyEvents.title: Walked in Ahab's ways
keyEvents.description: Ahaziah did what was evil in the Lord's sight. Through his mother Athaliah and advisors from Ahab's house, he was led into idolatry and Baal worship.

keyEvents.title: Allied with Joram of Israel against Aram
keyEvents.description: Ahaziah went with Joram, son of Ahab, to fight against Hazael, king of Aram, at Ramoth in Gilead. Joram was wounded in the battle.

keyEvents.title: Visited the wounded Joram in Jezreel
keyEvents.description: Ahaziah went down to Jezreel to visit King Joram of Israel, who had been wounded. This visit placed him right in the middle of Jehu's revolt against Ahab's house.

keyEvents.title: Killed during Jehu's revolt
keyEvents.description: During Jehu's revolt against Ahab's house, Ahaziah tried to flee. He was mortally wounded at the ascent to Gur near Ibleam and died in Megiddo. His servants then brought him to Jerusalem for burial. The books of Chronicles provide a supplementary account stating that Ahaziah was found while hiding in Samaria.

versions.summary: Ahaziah was the sixth king of Judah after the kingdom split, reigning only one year. He followed the evil example of his mother Athaliah and grandfather Ahab and worshiped Baal. He was killed by Jehu during his revolt against Ahab's house in Israel.
versions.title: Judah's short-reigning king
versions.reason: [minor] Ahaziah's lifespan is given as approx. 843-842 BC, but this covers only his reign. Since he was 22 years old when he became king (2 Kgs 8:26), the lifespan should reflect his entire life, thus approx. 865-842 BC. Note: 2 Chr 22:2 gives the age as 42 years, but this is generally considered a scribal error.; [minor] The description 'the sixth king of Judah after the division of the kingdom' can be debated. The order is: Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joram, Ahaziah – which makes him the sixth. This is correct.; [minor] Ahaziah was also a military ally with Israel in the war against Aram. One might consider adding 'military ally' or leaving it as just 'king' since this is covered by keyEvents.; [major] According to 2 Chr 21:17 and 22:1, Ahaziah's older brothers were killed by Philistines and Arabs in a raid, and Ahaziah became king as the youngest. Although the names of his brothers are not always known, it should be noted that he had brothers. In 2 Chr 21:2 several sons of Jehoshaphat are mentioned who include brothers of Joram, but Joram himself had sons who were killed. This should at least be remarked upon.; [minor] Ahaziah had at least one son (Joash), so he must have had at least one wife, even though her name is not certainly known. Some traditions identify her as Sibya from Beersheba (2 Kgs 12:1), the mother of Joash.; [minor] It could be useful to include an event from 2 Chronicles to give a more complete picture, e.g., 2 Chr 22:1 which explains why Ahaziah became king (the brothers were killed) and 2 Chr 22:7-9 which gives further details about his death.; [major] Footnotes are missing. There are several interesting historical, linguistic, and theological points related to Ahaziah that should be covered.; [minor] The age '22 years' according to 2 Kgs 8:26 versus '42 years' in 2 Chr 22:2 is a known textual critical issue that deserves a footnote.

versions.summary: Ahaziah was the sixth king of Judah after the kingdom split and the son of Joram and Athaliah, daughter of Israel's king Ahab. He became king after his older brothers were killed in a Philistine-Arab raid, and he reigned only one year in Jerusalem. Influenced by his mother and advisors from Ahab's house, he did what was evil in the Lord's sight and followed Baal worship. When he visited his relative King Joram of Israel in Jezreel, he was caught up in Jehu's revolt against Ahab's house and killed. His death paved the way for his mother Athaliah's coup and tyrannical rule over Judah.
versions.title: Judah's short-reigning king
versions.reason: [minor] Ahaziah had older brothers who were killed in the Philistine-Arabian raid (2 Chr 21:16-17). Although their names are not known with certainty, the field should not be left empty without comment. However, it is understandable that it is empty since the brothers are unnamed in the text.; [major] Zibiah (צִבְיָה) is mentioned in 2 Kgs 12:2 as the mother of Joash, but she is described as 'from Beersheba' and it is not entirely explicit that she was Ahaziah's wife (although this is the natural conclusion). The ID should be 'zibiah-from-beersheba' or simply 'zibiah' in lowercase. The current value 'zibiah' is acceptable as an ID format, but this is a reasonable interpretation.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but the phrasing 'the sixth king of Judah after the division of the kingdom' should be verified. Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joram, Ahaziah – it is correct that Ahaziah is the sixth. The phrasing is accurate.; [minor] The description of Ahaziah's death combines 2 Kgs 9:27-28 with 2 Chr 22:7-9 well, but it is worth noting that the account in Chronicles differs somewhat – there Ahaziah is found hiding in Samaria and brought to Jehu. The current description follows primarily the version in Kings, which is acceptable, but a nuance could be considered.; [minor] The role 'king' is correct, but can be supplemented with 'king of Judah' for increased precision and consistency with other king profiles.

versions.summary: Ahaziah, son of King Joram and Athaliah (granddaughter of Omri and daughter of Ahab), was the sixth king of Judah after the kingdom split. He came to power after all his older brothers were killed during a Philistine-Arabian attack, and he reigned only one year in Jerusalem. Under strong influence from his mother and advisors from Ahab's house, he pursued a policy marked by idolatry and Baal worship, continuing the destructive alliance between Judah and the royal house of northern Israel. When he visited his relative King Joram of Israel at Jezreel, he was caught up in Jehu's divinely sanctioned revolt against Ahab's dynasty and killed. His early death marked a turning point in Judah's history, as it paved the way for his mother Athaliah's coup—the only known case of a female sole ruler on David's throne.
versions.title: Judah's short-reigning king
versions.reason: [minor] Ahaziah had older brothers who were killed during the Philistine-Arabian attack (2 Chr 21:16-17). Although we do not know their names with certainty, it should be considered whether this needs to be commented on, or if it is sufficient that it is covered in keyEvents. The current empty array is acceptable since the brothers died before Ahaziah became king and their names are unknown.; [minor] Sibjah (from Beersheba) is known as the mother of Joash (2 Kgs 12:2), but the text does not explicitly confirm that she was married to Ahaziah – this is a reasonable inference, but it is worth noting that this is an indirect connection.; [minor] The phrasing "granddaughter of Omri and daughter of Ahab" can be somewhat confusing. Athaliah is referred to as "daughter of Omri" in 2 Kgs 8:26 (likely meaning descendant or relative) and "daughter of Ahab" in 2 Kgs 8:18. There is academic debate over whether she was Ahab's biological daughter or stepdaughter. A clarification would be useful.; [minor] The phrasing "According to 2 Kings" refers directly to a specific book. This is fine in this context, but it should consistently use the book reference neutrally. This has already been done here, but consider whether "According to the Books of Kings" would have been more consistent with the rest of the text.

footnotes.text: There is a well-known textual critical issue regarding Ahaziah's age. In 2 Kings 8:26, his age is given as 22 when he became king, while 2 Chronicles 22:2 gives 42 years. Most scholars consider 22 to be the original reading, since 42 would make him older than his father Joram, who died at age 40 (2 Chronicles 21:20). The discrepancy is usually explained as a scribal error in numerical symbols.

Ahaziah is also called 'Jehoahaz' (יהואחז) in 2 Chronicles 21:17 – an inverted form of the same name (אחזיה, Ahazyahu). Both names mean roughly the same thing: 'The Lord has seized' or 'Seized by the Lord.' Such name variations are common in Hebrew royal texts.

Jehu's revolt and the killing of Ahaziah are connected to the Tel Dan Stele, where King Hazael of Aram appears to claim he killed both Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah. This archaeological source offers an interesting counterpoint to the biblical account, which attributes the killings to Jehu. The discrepancy has been the subject of considerable academic debate.

Theologically, Ahaziah's fate is presented as a direct consequence of Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab's house through the marriage of Joram and Athaliah. Chronicles emphasizes that advisors from Ahab's house led Ahaziah to ruin (2 Chronicles 22:3-4), serving as a warning against alliances with ungodly rulers.

According to 2 Chronicles 21:16-17, Philistines and Arabs killed all of Joram's older sons in a raid, leaving only the youngest, Ahaziah (called Jehoahaz), alive. This explains why he specifically became Joram's successor as king over Judah.

Ahaziah's brief reign of just one year places him among a series of short-reigning kings during the divided monarchy period. His death at Jehu's hand was part of a larger purge of Ahab's dynastic influence, which also affected Joram of Israel and many other members of Ahab's extended family (2 Kings 10:12-14).

Ahaziah's kinship with Omri's dynasty through his mother Athaliah illustrates the complex dynastic marriages during the period of the divided monarchy. Such alliance marriages were common practice in the ancient Near East to strengthen political ties, but biblical authors consistently evaluate them negatively when they involve idolatrous royal houses.
